newsitem.title: USA: Armey slams police group's endorsement of Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Armey slams police group's endorsement of Clinton.

text.p: House Republican Leader Dick Armey criticised the Fraternal Order of Police Tuesday for endorsing President Clinton's re-election bid, terming their members a union mob "dressed up like policemen."
The 270,000-member group, the nation's largest police organisation, endorsed Clinton Monday at a rally in Cincinnati. It had backed Republican George Bush in 1992.

Armey, the No. 2 House Republican, said he watched television news accounts of the endorsement and "I got the biggest kick out of the networks. ... They trot out President Clinton with his mob of union members behind him dressed up like policemen."
The Texas Republican charged the group had based its endorsement mainly on organised labour's concerns, rather than on bread-and-butter law enforcement issues.

To bolster his case, he pointed to statements by Gilbert Gallegos, president of the Fraternal Order of Police, who said Clinton's support of due process rights, salary and other labour issues had played a big role in the decision.

"This is an unsophisticated union. Ordinarily, as you know, unions wrap their politics of greed in the language of love. This guy just dropped the language of love and said right from the outset, 'Labor is our principal issue,'" Armey said. "The Fraternal Order of Police, another union endorsing Bill Clinton, did not impress me as particularly startling news."

Clinton, who has been attacked by Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole as soft on crime, worked hard to win the police group's support. He has attended its annual memorials for slain officers, and he held a special White House meeting with its officials last week.
Clinton won the coveted endorsement on the day Dole made a major speech on crime in Pennsylvania, undercutting the Republican's tough law-and-order rhetoric.
Jim Pasco, executive director of the Fraternal Order of Police, rejected Armey's statements, saying law-and-order issues played a major role in the group's decision.

"Law-and-order issues were every bit as important as labour issues in endorsing President Clinton, as Mr. Armey would know if he read our release or listened to Mr. Gallegos' remarks," Pasco said. "Mr. Armey is reacting in a partisan fashion to an endorsement that was given by a nonpartisan organisation."
About half the group's members belong to unions and are represented in contract talks by the organisation. But a significant number are federal officers, who cannot engage in collective bargaining.
